title: Fatigue Behavior and Fractographic Analysis of Low-Carbon Steel Fabricated by CMT-Based Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing
abstract: Abstract Wire arc additive manufacturing (WAAM) using the cold metal transfer (CMT) process offers significant advantages for producing large and complex metal components. However, the thermal cycles inherent to layer-by-layer deposition induce variations in microstructure and mechanical properties, which critically affect fatigue behavior and fracture mechanisms. This study evaluates the fatigue resistance and fracture characteristics of ER70S-6 steel deposited by CMT-WAAM. Fatigue tests were performed on seven specimens extracted in the horizontal orientation relative to the deposition direction, under a load ratio of  R  = 0.1 and a frequency of 20 Hz. The results indicate a fatigue limit of approximately 302 MPa (≈ 0.53 Su), consistent with typical behavior of low-alloy steels. The reuse of a previously tested specimen resulted in a significant reduction in fatigue life, confirming the detrimental effect of prior fatigue damage. Fractographic analysis via SEM revealed crack initiation at defects, followed by propagation characterized by striations and final fracture dominated by ductile dimples. At the highest stress level (0.67 Su), a less distinct fracture pattern and increased ductile features were observed, indicating accelerated crack propagation. The results highlight the dominant role of defects, stress level, and loading history in controlling fatigue performance, providing relevant insights for improving the reliability of WAAM components under cyclic loading.
journal: Journal of Materials Engineering and Performance

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Additive manufacturing (AM) processes have been increasingly adopted and investigated to meet the constant demand for production optimization, cost reduction, and alternative fabrication methods. Dilberoglu et al. (Ref  1 ) highlight the relevance of AM within the context of Industry 4.0, emphasizing its ability to enable product customization and the creation of complex designs that are otherwise unattainable through conventional manufacturing techniques. In a recent review, Selema et al. (Ref  2 ) discussed current trends and advancements in metal additive manufacturing, pointing out key advantages such as design optimization, mass reduction, and the environmentally friendly nature of the process due to minimal material waste, and its suitability for producing small batches of components with complex geometries.

Despite these advantages, additive manufacturing still presents important challenges that may affect its broader implementation. The digital nature of AM enables the easy replication and distribution of design files, which can compromise the protection of proprietary models. In addition, sustainability remains a relevant concern, particularly regarding the high energy demand of certain processes, the limited recyclability of some materials, and the end-of-life management of printed components. These aspects highlight the need for continued investigation to ensure the efficient and responsible application of AM technologies (Ref  3 ). In parallel, additive manufacturing has shown significant potential in component remanufacturing, particularly for the repair and restoration of damaged parts. The integration of technologies such as reverse engineering enables accurate identification and reconstruction of worn regions, supporting efficient material deposition and geometry recovery. Processes based on directed energy deposition, especially laser-based techniques, are widely applied due to their ability to restore components with satisfactory mechanical performance and reduced material usage. However, challenges remain regarding process selection, material compatibility, and the control of repair quality, including surface finish, geometric accuracy, and repeatability (Ref  4 ).

Within the AM processes that are classified as directed energy deposition, wire arc additive manufacturing (WAAM) is a group of deposition technologies able to produce parts with large dimensions, with relatively lower power consumption and shorter lead times (Ref  5 ). Among the various metal WAAM processes, the cold metal transfer (CMT) method stands out. It is a variation of the gas metal arc welding (GMAW) process and allows high deposition rates when compared with other additive manufacturing techniques. However, CMT offers improved deposition control through mechanical droplet detachment via wire retraction, which results in lower heat input and consequently better deposition quality. This mechanism also significantly reduces spatter formation (Ref  6 ) and provides better control of the weld pool (Ref  7 ).

From an electrical perspective, the cold metal transfer (CMT) process can be divided into three phases. The first phase involves an increase in current associated with constant voltage, which initiates the electric arc and forms a droplet. The second phase is marked by a reduction in current to prevent globular transfer. Finally, during the short-circuit phase, the wire makes contact with the molten pool. At this point, the voltage drops to near zero, triggering a signal to the controller, which then activates the servomotor responsible for retracting the wire (Ref  8 ). A broader perspective on WAAM process fundamentals can be obtained by considering alternative GMAW-based variants and their influence on heat input and deposition behavior. The cold metal transfer (CMT) process, developed by Fronius (Ref  9 ), employs controlled droplet detachment through wire retraction after a short circuit, allowing material transfer at reduced current and voltage levels. In contrast, processes such as double-electrode GMAW (DE-GMAW) and tandem GMAW (T-GMAW) utilize multiple electrodes to increase productivity, generally resulting in higher and more complex thermal input. Alternating current GMAW (AC-GMAW) combines electrode polarities to balance melting efficiency and weld quality (Ref  9 ). Compared to these variants, CMT is associated with reduced thermal input, which contributes to lower residual stresses and distortion, as well as improved deposition stability (Ref  10 ). In this context, Nagasai et al. (Ref  11 ) demonstrated that CMT can achieve comparable or higher deposition rates than conventional GMAW while maintaining better control over the process, leading to improved mechanical performance due to differences in thermal history and resulting microstructure.

Regardless, this is a process in which the part is subjected to high heat, and each layer will be subjected to a different thermal load since the thermal input, and the heat exchange vary with the deposition (Ref  12 ). The deposition thermal characteristics can result in geometrical (Ref  13 ), microstructural (Ref  14 ), and microhardness (Ref  15 ) variations. These variations and possible defects during deposition can hinder the application of the part (Ref  16 ). The work of Kumar et al. (Ref  17 ) exemplifies this variation. The deposition was carried out using the WAAM-GMAW process with ER70S-6 wire, producing circular and rectangular components. Vickers microhardness measurements were taken in different regions of the parts. The results showed average Vickers microhardness values of 168.806, 163.473, and 172.191 HV for the straight section, edge, and curved section of the rectangular parts, respectively. A higher microhardness was observed at the top regions of the components, which is attributed to the higher cooling rates in these areas. Additionally, the circular deposition exhibited higher average microhardness compared to the rectangular ones, likely due to a more uniform heat distribution throughout the deposition process.

Additional evidence of the influence of thermal cycles on hardness distribution and microstructural evolution in WAAM components is provided by Costa et al. (Ref  15 ), who performed a vertical microhardness analysis based on column-wise averaging along the wall thickness. Their results demonstrated that deposition strategy and thermal management significantly affect hardness levels. In particular, bidirectional deposition without temperature control resulted in higher average microhardness, whereas the application of interlayer temperature control led to lower values. Unidirectional deposition conditions showed intermediate behavior. The authors also observed that the relatively uniform uncertainty intervals along each column indicate that microstructural variation occurs predominantly along the build height rather than across the wall thickness. This behavior is consistent with Safarzade et al. (Ref  18 ), who reported that grain growth follows the direction of the maximum thermal gradient, typically aligned with the build direction. Furthermore, Kumar et al. (Ref  17 ) and Das et al. (Ref  19 ) identified distinct microstructural regions along the height, including martensitic structures in the upper regions, transition zones in the central region, and equiaxed or ferritic structures near the base. These findings reinforce that the thermal history inherent to WAAM processes governs hardness variation and microstructural heterogeneity, directly impacting the mechanical performance of the deposited material.

Therefore, for industrial applications, there is a significant demand for studies focused on the properties and suitable additive manufacturing techniques to ensure the required design specifications (Ref  20 ). Beyond the mechanical properties mentioned above that must be evaluated for additive manufacturing processes, fatigue resistance is critical for various applications, as most mechanical components are subjected to cyclic loading and are impacted by deposition (Ref  16 ). Fatigue is a phenomenon that results from cyclic loading on a material, and this type of failure is commonly observed in numerous mechanical applications (e.g., shafts, aircraft, gears, springs), as components are subjected to some level of dynamic stress. The cyclic stresses that cause fatigue can arise from axial, bending, or torsional loads and are influenced by variations in stress over time, including maximum, minimum, and mean stress values (Ref  21 ). Despite advances in fatigue modeling, the evaluation of materials with small defects under multiaxial loading remains challenging (Ref  22 ). An essential tool for fatigue analysis is the S-N curve, which relates stress (fatigue strength) to the number of cycles to failure. This curve is generated from a series of tests on standardized specimens, typically using pure bending loads (Ref  23 ). Unlike static failure, fatigue failure tends to occur suddenly, similar to brittle fracture, with little to no plastic deformation (Ref  23 ). According to Dowling (Ref  24 ), fatigue can be categorized according to the number of cycles: high-cycle fatigue occurs under a large number of cycles (in the millions) and is primarily elastic in nature, whereas low-cycle fatigue involves fewer cycles and is more associated with plastic deformation.

Sales et al. (Ref  25 ) investigated the fatigue strength of super duplex stainless steel. To this end, the authors deposited wall structures using ER2594 wire in the CMT process. Specimens were then extracted from these walls and subjected to fatigue testing at a frequency of 10 Hz and a load ratio of  R  = 0.1. Based on these tests and additional data from other alloys, an S-N curve was established. The results indicated that the longitudinal specimens exhibited higher fatigue strength, revealing significant material anisotropy. Similarly, Ermakova et al. (Ref  26 ) deposited a wall structure using ER100S-1 wire in the CMT process and extracted specimens in both vertical and horizontal orientations relative to the deposition direction. Fatigue tests were conducted at a load ratio of  R  = 0.1 and a frequency of 5 Hz to analyze crack propagation behavior. The study revealed that specimen orientation influenced crack propagation. Additionally, ductile fracture was observed in specimens extracted in both directions.

In other work, Ermakova et al. (Ref  27 ) used ER70S-6 wire and the CMT process to deposit a wall structure, aiming to evaluate fatigue crack growth. The tests were conducted using a load ratio of  R  = 0.1, a sinusoidal waveform at a frequency of 5 Hz, and maximum loads of 10 and 11 kN. Crack growth was monitored using a high-resolution camera positioned in front of the testing machine. The initial crack length of the specimens was approximately 20 mm. The results showed that for a 10-kN load, horizontally oriented specimens exhibited twice the fatigue resistance of vertically oriented ones. However, under an 11 kN load, the opposite behavior was observed, with vertical specimens demonstrating higher fatigue resistance. These findings suggest that the deposition direction may not have a significant effect on fatigue crack growth.

In summary, while wire arc additive manufacturing using the cold metal transfer process offers promising advantages in terms of deposition control, material efficiency, and geometric flexibility, challenges related to thermal effects, microstructural variations, and mechanical performance, particularly fatigue and fracture behavior, remain critical considerations. Understanding these aspects is essential to ensure the reliability and structural integrity of WAAM-produced components for industrial applications. Therefore, this study focuses on characterizing the fatigue resistance and fracture behavior of ER70S-6 steel deposited via the CMT process, aiming to provide insights that support optimized process parameters and informed material selection.

Besides what is already in the literature, most of the available literature focuses on anisotropy effects, crack growth behavior, or the influence of post-processing techniques, often under specific deposition conditions such as higher wire feed speeds or hybrid processing routes. In contrast, the present study evaluates the fatigue response of CMT-WAAM ER70S-6 steel produced under a low wire feed speed and continuous deposition over 100 layers, resulting in distinct thermal accumulation and microstructural conditions. Additionally, fatigue tests were conducted using miniaturized specimens extracted from the deposited wall without post-processing, enabling the assessment of as-deposited material behavior. The study further combines S-N characterization with detailed SEM fractographic analysis, allowing the identification of crack initiation mechanisms and their relationship with process-induced defects. Therefore, the contribution of this work lies in providing an integrated evaluation of fatigue behavior and fracture mechanisms under a specific and less explored processing condition, with emphasis on the role of defects in controlling fatigue performance. Thus, considering that WAAM-deposited materials still need further investigation on mechanical properties, to contribute to their understanding, this work aims to not only evaluate fatigue resistance but also fracture behavior of the ER70S-6 deposited steel.

sections.heading: Materials and Methods
paragraphs: The deposition methodology was based on the best parameters obtained in the work of Novelino et al. (Ref  7 ). The power source was a Fronius TransPuls Synergic 5000 CMT, configured for GMAW-CMT. The source was associated with a Cartesian robot Schneider Electric MAXR23-S42-H42-C42 with an operational range of 800 mm in width, 800 mm in length, and 500 mm in height. The protection gas selected for the GMAW-CMT process was applied at 20 l/min flow, with composition containing Ar + 18%CO 2 . The substrate was an AISI 1020 steel plate, with a current of 65 A and synergic mode for the voltage, the wire feed speed (WFS) was maintained constant at 2.6 m/min, the torch travel speed (TTS) was also constant, being 8 mm/s in the horizontal direction and 24 mm/s in the vertical direction. The wall was deposited with a bidirectional strategy; the 100 layers were deposited without interruptions and the step over between layers was set as 1.2 mm. Figure  1  illustrates the deposition parameters and the deposited wall. Fig. 1 Material deposition, (a) Scheme of the deposition with parameters and (b) deposited wall

The material deposited was the ER70S-6, having a chemical composition of 0.07% C, 0.85% Si, and 1.50% Mn (Ref  28 ). The mechanical properties can be observed on Table  1 .
 Table 1 Typical mechanical properties (Ref  28 ) Yield strength, MPa Tensile strength, MPa Elongation, % Charpy impact strength - J 450 575 Min 30 27 Min (− 30C)

After the walls were fabricated using the CMT method, test specimens were extracted in accordance with the conditions and dimensions specified by ASTM E466 (Ref  29 ). The specimen geometry with a rectangular cross section was selected, as it is considered the most suitable for miniature specimens. In Fig.  2 (a), it is possible to observe the standard geometry for the specimen, and in Fig.  2 (b), it is possible to observe a representation of how the specimens were positioned on the wall, with respect to the deposition direction. To obtain all the dimensions, starting from a predefined thickness, obtained by the wall dimension and the necessary material removal for surface finishing, the remaining dimensions were calculated based on the relationships provided in the standard. The specimen dimensions are presented in Table  2 . Fig. 2 Specimens’ dimensions (a) Standard dimensions and (b) representation of specimens’ positioning Table 2 Dimensions based on ASTM E466 (Ref  29 ) Thickness, T Width, W Gage length, L Filet radius, R Cross-sectional area 2.00 mm 4.00 mm 8.00 mm 32.00 mm 8.00 mm 2

The preparation of the specimens followed five steps: Deposition of the walls  Two 100 layer walls were deposited with the same parameters. Substrate removal  The substrate was removed with a Franho FM-500 bandsaw machine equipped with an FM 500 Bi-Alpha Cobalt blade. Surface milling  was performed perpendicular to the deposition direction, with a total of nine passes on each side, with a 0.5-mm depth of cut per pass. The process parameters, cutting speed, feed rate, and spindle speed, were set at 89.54 m/min, 0.57 m/min, and 2850 rpm, respectively. These parameters were selected based on the results of a preliminary test. The machine tool was a CNC VEGA XH7132, and the cutting tool was a four-flute uncoated carbide mill, Dormer C247, with a 10-mm diameter. Water jet cutting  To obtain the standard geometry, the specimens were cut using CNC water jet, avoiding possible thermal damage from other processes like electrical discharge machining (EDM). Surface finishing  Prior to the fatigue trials, the specimens were also subjected to a cleaning process using a circular steel brush (EN 1083-2).

After machining, the surface roughness was measured using a Mitutoyo® roughness tester, with a cutoff length of 2.5 mm. Three specimens were randomly selected, and 9 measurements were performed in each. The roughness parameters arithmetic mean roughness (Ra), mean peak-to-valley height (Rz), and root mean square roughness (Rq) were evaluated, following the criteria adopted by Todhunter et al. (Ref  30 ). After machining, the surface obtained possessed the following roughness values: Ra = 5.56 ± 1.43 µm, Rq = 30.81 ± 4.57 µm, and Rz = 6.86 ± 1.75 µm. The surface condition was intentionally kept as-machined, without polishing, to better represent in-service conditions, as polishing could hinder the visualization and analysis of defect propagation influenced by surface features. Besides not being the focus of the study, the microstructure was evaluated to assess the material condition prior to the fatigue tests and ensure no excessive defects occurred during the deposition. For this, the specimen preparation involved extraction of an intermediate region to represent the wall. This specimen was then cold mounted and subjected to sequential wet sanding to minimize defects from extraction and the original surface. Polishing was performed using abrasive paste to obtain a smooth, defect-free, mirror-like surface. Finally, chemical etching was carried out using nitric acid to reveal the microstructure, Fig.  3 . The microstructure reveals a predominance of coarse grains, representing the largest portion of the observed microstructure in the cross-sectional profile. The microstructure is mainly composed of polygonal ferrite, visible as lighter and elongated regions along the grain boundaries, surrounding pearlite colonies. It is worth mentioning that this microstructure is only a qualitative representation of the wall since studies have shown that near the substrate and in the last layers higher thermal variation can occur. Fig. 3 Material microstructure

Vickers’ microhardness (HV) was also evaluated; DuraScan (EMCO TEST) equipment was used with 10 × and 40 × lenses. The test employed a square-based pyramidal diamond indenter with a 136° angle between faces, an indentation speed of up to 0.200 mm/s, a dwell time of 7 s, and an applied load of 0.5 kgf. The resulting HV was 140.55 ± 36.36, which is lower than the one presented by Costa et al. (Ref  15 ), who obtained values around 200 HV for the same material and different deposition methods. It is worth mentioning that those authors deposited a small wall with only 26; thus the difference might be due to the lower thermal gradients in the wall of the present study, which can also be associated with the coarse grains of the microstructure. It should be highlighted that the microstructural evaluation presented in this study is limited to a qualitative assessment of the deposited material and is not intended to establish a direct relationship with fatigue behavior. Its purpose is to confirm the general material condition prior to testing, while the fatigue performance is primarily discussed based on mechanical results and fractographic observations.

The anisotropy of WAAM-fabricated steels is intrinsically associated with the layer-by-layer deposition process and the resulting thermal gradients along the build direction. Both studies indicate that, although microstructural variations exist between the top, middle, and bottom regions due to differences in cooling rates and reheating cycles, the overall anisotropy is relatively limited. The microstructure remains predominantly composed of bainitic ferrite, martensite, and retained austenite throughout the build height, with only slight variations in phase distribution and grain refinement (Ref  31 ). Consequently, the mechanical properties exhibit near-isotropic behavior, with relatively uniform hardness, tensile strength, and impact toughness, albeit with minor directional differences, particularly in yield strength and impact energy (Ref  31 ). Additionally, variations in process conditions, such as arc mode, influence thermal cycling and heat input, thereby affecting microstructural homogeneity and residual stress distribution; however, even under different deposition strategies, the resulting anisotropy remains low due to the repeated remelting and tempering inherent to the WAAM process (Ref  32 ).

Regarding deposition direction, specimens extracted along different orientations (horizontal, vertical, and inclined) may present measurable differences in mechanical response, mainly due to the alignment of microstructural features and the influence of interlayer boundaries relative to the loading direction. In particular, vertically oriented specimens tend to be more sensitive to interlayer interfaces and thermal gradients, whereas horizontal specimens better represent the in-layer material behavior and exhibit more homogeneous properties (Ref  31 ). In the present research, in addition to acknowledging the presence of anisotropy, only horizontal specimens were considered for evaluation. This decision is supported by the fact that WAAM components are often deposited following a preferential direction, and the horizontal orientation provides a more consistent and representative assessment of intrinsic material properties, while minimizing the influence of interlayer effects associated with the build direction.

For the fatigue tests, an MTS Landmark servo-hydraulic testing system, model 370.10 (Ref  33 ), was used. This equipment was selected due to its capability for dynamic loading with lower amplitudes compared to other models. An essential requirement is that the use of specimens with smaller cross sections requires the application of lower forces. For specimen clamping, a 647.10 Wedge Set Assy was employed, which is suitable for specimen thicknesses ranging from 0 to 7.6 mm (Ref  34 ). Figure  4  shows the fixture used to perform the fatigue tests. Tests were carried out at the controlled ambient temperature (24 ± 2 °C) and humidity (45-55%). Moreover, the temperature at the gauge length zone was monitored using a thermographic camera (FLIR C5-C8940) as detailed in (Ref  35 ). No self-heating was observed during the tests. Fig. 4 Fatigue test (a) Side view of the specimen and (b) front view of the specimen

The specimens were subjected to uniaxial fatigue testing at a load ratio of  R  = 0.1, based on similar tests found in the literature (Ref  36 ,  37 - 38 ). The frequency was also determined based on previous studies. In the aforementioned works, the applied frequencies were 50, 10, and 5 Hz, respectively. Therefore, an initial frequency of 5 Hz was adopted for this study. However, since increasing the frequency did not compromise signal quality measured by the testing system, a final value of 20 Hz was used as the standard for all tests. The frequency variation did not affect the results, since for metallic materials in the high-cycle fatigue regime, and in the absence of significant self-heating, the influence of testing frequency within this range is generally negligible, as reported in the literature (Ref  39 ,  40 ).

As a starting point for the S-N curve, a stress value corresponding to 61% of the material’s ultimate tensile strength (350 MPa) was calculated and used as a baseline. From this point, subsequent stress levels were selected to ensure a well-distributed set of data points along the curve. This allowed the construction of the S-N curve representing the material’s fatigue life. It should be noted that the fatigue analysis is based on a limited dataset, with only six valid data points used to construct the S-N curve. This number is insufficient for a statistically robust definition of the S-N relationship or for determining the fatigue limit. In addition, no repeated tests were performed at the same stress levels, which prevent the evaluation of data scatter and statistical confidence. Therefore, the results should be interpreted as indicative of fatigue behavior trends rather than definitive material properties.

For image-based evaluation of the fracture region, a JSM-7100F scanning electron microscope (SEM) was used. The halves of each fractured specimen were prepared and analyzed with respect to surface morphology, presence of discontinuities, and topographical features, enabling the characterization of fatigue failure.

sections.heading: S-N Curve and Fatigue Results
paragraphs:
The fatigue tests were conducted using the following parameters: a frequency of 20 Hz, a load ratio of  R  = 0.1, and load levels that varied according to the responses obtained in each test, as established in the experimental design. After applying a stress of 350 MPa as the starting point (0.61Su), the tests were conducted according to the sequence shown in Table  3 . The table lists the tests in the order they were performed, the specimen used, the maximum applied stress, the ratio of the applied stress to the ultimate tensile strength of the material (Su), and the results obtained. A threshold of one million cycles was adopted as the criterion for infinite fatigue life. Specimens 2 and 7 reached this runout criterion while the remaining specimens displayed rupture. It is important to emphasize that despite the reduced number of tests, the obtained S-N curve (depicted in Fig.  5 ) shows a consistent trendline ( R 2  = 91%) and a relatively low scatter (± 40%). Specimen SP2 was subsequently retested (test 7) at the same stress level to qualitatively assess the effect of prior fatigue damage. A significant reduction in fatigue life was observed compared to its initial response, indicating damage accumulation within the material. This additional test was treated as an auxiliary evaluation and was not included in the construction of the S-N curve.
 Table 3 Fatigue results for horizontal specimens Test Specimen Maximum stress, Mpa Stress ratio Cycles 1 SP6 350.00 0.61Su 275000 2 SP1 384.00 0.67Su 174105 3 SP3 316.80 0.55Su 423650 4 SP2 283.20 0.49Su 1200000 (runout) 5 SP5 316.80 0.55Su 731704 6 SP7 302.04 0.53Su 1200000 (runout) Fig. 5 S-N curve obtained from fatigue tests

This behavior was similarly observed in the research of Kanishka and Acherjee (Ref  41 ), where the authors compared low-carbon steel plates repaired with ER70S-6 steel wire via GMAW-WAAM. It was noted that the WAAM, despite exhibiting higher tensile strength, showed lower fatigue strength and endurance (100 MPa) compared to the base material (110 MPa). Fractographic analysis indicated that fatigue failure in WAAM samples was primarily governed by crack initiation at surface irregularities, edges, and internal pores, while base specimens consistently initiated cracks at edge regions with high stress concentration. This behavior aligns with literature reports identifying defect-driven mechanisms as dominant in fatigue behavior of WAAM-processed ER70S-6 steels.

For comparison to the obtained result, the article published by Dirisu et al. (Ref  37 ) was consulted; it addresses the fatigue strength of ERS70-6 wire specimens (the same material used in this work) manufactured by the CMT method and by the hybrid CMT method combined with rolling. For the fatigue test, the authors used the same load ratio as in the current work,  R  = 0.1, but with a frequency of 10 Hz, which is half of that used in the present study. The results of those authors showed that the infinite life for the machined specimens was achieved at stresses below 350 MPa, whereas in this work a stress of 350 MPa led to a fatigue life of 275,000 cycles, with infinite life occurring from 302.04 MPa onwards (test 6).

It is worth emphasizing that the comparison between the studies can only be made qualitatively, since the parameters used in the deposition process were different, resulting in parts with different properties. In this case, the main discrepancy was the wire feed speed, which was roughly 2.4 times higher in the study by Dirisu et al. (Ref  37 ,  42 ). This relationship may suggest that a higher wire feed speed leads to improved fatigue resistance; however, due to the large number of process variables, this correlation requires further investigation for confirmation.

According to Norton (Ref  42 ), one method to estimate the fatigue limit, defined as the stress level below which fatigue failure does not occur, is based on the material’s tensile strength limit. For steels, the fatigue limit is typically half of the tensile strength limit. Considering that in this study infinite life began at a stress of 302.04 MPa and using the properties provided in Table  1 , a ratio of 0.525 is obtained between the fatigue limit and the tensile strength limit, indicating close agreement with the theoretical estimate. Nonetheless, due to material availability constraints, six fatigue data points were considered sufficient to establish a consistent trend in the S-N response; the curve was accordingly refined and the reported fatigue limit of 302 MPa is supported by the observed repeatability and coherence of the results.

Overall, the S-N behavior obtained for the horizontally extracted specimens indicates a transition between finite and infinite fatigue life in the stress range between 0.55 and 0.49 Su. The results show a consistent reduction in fatigue life with increasing stress amplitude, as well as sensitivity to prior fatigue damage, as evidenced by the reuse of specimen 2. The experimentally estimated fatigue limit is in agreement with theoretical expectations based on tensile strength. However, these findings are restricted to horizontally extracted, as-deposited WAAM-CMT ER70S-6 specimens and do not account for potential variations associated with different build orientations, base material conditions, or post-processing treatments. Therefore, the results should be interpreted within this specific context.

sections.heading: Fracture Evaluation
paragraphs: The evaluation of the fracture region using SEM revealed important characteristics of fatigue failure in the specimens. Of the four fractured SPs, three exhibited very similar characteristics, with well-defined regions (SP3, SP5, and SP6), while SP1 exhibited visibly different behavior from the others. One indicator of crack propagation during the fatigue process is the presence of dimple regions and cleavage regions. Dimple regions characterize ductile fracture, while cleavage regions are indicative of brittle fracture (Ref  43 ). Mattos et al. (Ref  44 ) note that the beginning and end of fatigue fracture can be represented, respectively, by striations (indicative of fatigue crack propagation) at the beginning and dimples at the end of fatigue fracture.

SEM results for SP3 are presented in Fig.  6 . Striations are observed in the left region (images 1 and 6), indicating crack propagation from a probable initiation site associated with a stress concentrator identified in image 1. In contrast, the right region presents a more irregular morphology, where dimpled features characteristic of ductile fracture are predominant, corresponding to the final stage of failure. Additionally, porosity is evident in this region, as highlighted in images 7, 8, 9, and 10. Fig. 6 Images of the fracture section of SP3 obtained through SEM

In addition to the section images, the rupture profile was also evaluated, shown in Fig.  7 . In it, it is possible to see the delimitation of a deeper region, equivalent to the striation region, and a higher region, equivalent to the ductile fracture region (dimples). Silva et al. (Ref  45 ) evaluated ER70S-6 produced by WAAM-CMT using Gurson’s porous material model to describe the influence of porosity on mechanical behavior. The study reported porosity levels between 5 and 18%, with a strong effect on yield strength, elastic modulus, and ductility. A clear anisotropic response was observed, with specimens built in the L direction showing higher ductility (plastic strain ~ 1.0-1.3), while T-direction specimens exhibited significantly lower ductility (≈ 40% of L), attributed to void elongation and directional solidification. Similarly, the present work observed that porosity and other discontinuities govern mechanical performance under fatigue, acting as crack initiation sites and controlling crack propagation. Although final fracture was predominantly ductile (dimpled morphology), defects as described in (Ref  45 ) can influence local stress concentration and crack growth behavior. Fig. 7 Images of the rupture profile of SP3 obtained through SEM

Other studies on WAAM components further support these observations. Rodrigues et al. (Ref  46 ) investigated HSLA steel deposited by WAAM and evaluated the influence of thermal cycles on material properties. The authors reported that the deposition of successive layers affects previously deposited ones by reducing the cooling rate, which contributes to microstructural refinement and a reduction in defects such as cracks. They also emphasized that, in the absence of geometric constraints, the material can better accommodate residual stresses, which is beneficial for structural integrity. However, they noted that the final layers experience fewer reheating cycles and consequently higher cooling rates, which may lead to microstructural heterogeneity. This effect can influence defect distribution and evolution and therefore plays an important role in crack initiation and propagation behavior under fatigue loading, as observed in the present study. Complementary for other ferrous alloys, Ola et al. (Ref  10 ) reinforce that using CMT reduces the thermal cycles and residual stresses associated with the deposition. Nonetheless, even the machining processes to which the part is submitted will influence the residual stresses (Ref  47 ), thus further investigation is suggested for future work.

Analysis of fracture mechanisms after fatigue failure is an essential step in understanding the type of failure that the material will present in practical applications. This type of behavior can vary according to the orientation and geometry of the specimens and the test parameters used (type of loading, load ratio, number of cycles, and frequency). There are types of discontinuities and defects that affect fatigue life, such as porosity, as observed by Biswal et al. (Ref  36 ) and Sales, Kotousov and Yin (Ref  25 ), and inclusions observed by Ayan and Kahraman (Ref  48 ). These discontinuities are often responsible for the initiation and growth of cracks, leading to premature failure of the material. Another element that can negatively affect fatigue is oxidation, as reported by Ron et al. (Ref  49 ). In their study, fatigue tests were conducted on a rotating beam for the ER70S-6 wire in a corrosive environment (NaCl solution) and in air. After the fatigue tests, specimens in a corrosive environment exhibited a significant reduction in fatigue resistance, and for 108 cycles, the resistance for the specimen in saline solution and in air was 140 and 220 MPa, respectively.

Building upon these observations, the effect of deposition strategy on microstructure and fracture behavior is further evidenced by studies incorporating torch oscillation in pulsed arc GMAW-WAAM of HSLA steels (Ref  50 ). According to Kumari et al. (Ref  50 ), the application of oscillation promotes microstructural refinement, reducing crystallite size from approximately 35.20-38.90 nm to 27.62-37.45 nm across the build height, while also increasing compressive residual stresses (e.g., from − 134.2 to − 171.5 MPa at the top region and from − 288.4 to − 331.2 MPa at the bottom). These changes are associated with improved mechanical performance, including increases in yield strength from ~ 505 to ~ 526 MPa and ultimate tensile strength from ~ 793 to ~ 816 MPa in the horizontal direction, alongside a reduction in elongation from ~ 32.9 to ~ 27.5%. Fractographic analysis indicates a transition toward more uniform ductile fracture surfaces with finer dimples, reflecting reduced defect influence. Additionally, impact toughness shows orientation-dependent behavior, with improvements of up to ~ 12% in the vertical direction. Collectively, these results demonstrate that enhanced thermal control and microstructural homogeneity directly reduce defect sensitivity, thereby limiting crack initiation and contributing to improved fatigue-relevant performance. This indicates that further studies could benefit from those different approaches in order to improve the fatigue life.

Figure  8 , region 1 shows the crack initiation site, where striations indicative of crack propagation are clearly observed, suggesting a predominantly brittle fracture behavior in this area. The crack growth direction is perpendicular to the striations (marked by the blue dashed lines), extending across the entire left region of the specimen. Fig. 8 Detail of SP3

Figure  9  shows regions of brittle fracture with visible striations. In Fig.  9 (a), the striations are almost parallel, with a crack growth direction consistent with that observed in Fig.  6 . Figure  9 (b) shows the transition region between the brittle (right) and ductile (left) fracture zones, containing the dimple structure. Fig. 9 Regions of fragile fracture and transition (a) Region 2 of SP3 and (b) Region 3 of SP3

Figure  10  shows auxiliary photographs taken from the other part of the specimen. Figure  10 (a) shows a structure consistent with an inclusion (which may have caused the crack to begin) or residue in the specimen. Figure  10 (b) shows a structure consistent with a pore, but it is not possible to say whether this is truly porosity, since the surrounding dimple structure can be easily confused. Verifying porosity and other discontinuities is fundamental for fatigue evaluation. A recent study from Araujo et al. (Ref  51 ) presents a new multiaxial fatigue model for materials containing small defects, presenting it as a modification of the classical SWT model. This model incorporates the √area parameter to account for defect size and relates it to principal stress components, specifically, the amplitude and maximum principal stresses, using the maximum variance method. Notably, the model addresses the challenge of estimating stress amplitude under complex loading conditions. When validated against experimental data from AISI 4140 steel under various loading modes (uniaxial, in-phase, and out-of-phase multiaxial), and using both smooth and micro-defected specimens, the model demonstrated slightly conservative predictions with average errors not exceeding 6%. This indicates that further research could apply this type of evaluation to WAAM materials. Fig. 10 Dimples and possible discontinuities on SP3, (a) Inclusion on the dimple region and (b) porosity

Like SP3, SP5 also showed a clear distinction between the regions of crack propagation and final rupture (Fig.  11 ). It is worth mentioning that specimen 5 was subjected to 731704 cycles and a maximum stress of 316.8 MPa before fracture (same stress value as SP3). The left region presents striations associated with crack propagation, indicating that crack initiation likely occurred at a stress concentrator located at the end of image 1. Image 8 shows the transition from brittle fracture (left) to ductile fracture (right). The right region is characterized by a dimpled morphology, as detailed in image 7. Fig. 11 Images of the fracture section of SP5 obtained through SEM

The profile images of SP5 (Fig.  12 ) also revealed a lower brittle fracture region compared with the ductile fracture region, displaying a pattern very similar to SP3, which was expected, given that both underwent the fatigue test with the same parameters. Fig. 12 Images of the rupture profile of SP5 obtained through SEM

In Fig.  13 , the fracture surface distinguishes ductile and brittle regions: the ductile region exhibits a rough, dimpled morphology, while the brittle region shows a striated surface. The profile view of the fractured specimen also indicates that these fracture modes occur on different planes, as observed in SP3. Fig. 13 Details of ductile and fragile fracture for SP5 (a) Fracture region and (b) profile view

Regions 1, 2 and 4, shown in Fig.  14 , contain striation marks along their entire length, indicating both brittle fracture and crack initiation. In Fig.  14 (a), striations are observed in different orientations, indicating multiple cracks, one of them at the corner of the part, at a geometric stress concentrator. Another possible origin of the crack is shown in Fig.  14 (c), close to the transition between the ductile and brittle regions. The crack originating in Fig.  14 (c) propagates to the region in Fig.  14 (b), perpendicular to the striations apparent in the part. Fig. 14 Details of striation marks on SP5 (a) Region 1, (b) Region 2, and (c) Region 4

Specimen 6 (SP6) was subjected to 274,417 cycles and a maximum stress of 350 MPa before fracture. By evaluating the fracture images of specimen 6 (Fig.  15 ), the cleavage region on the left was noted, where the striations showed an almost horizontal orientation (image 4, Fig.  15 ), unlike what occurred for example, in image 1 of Fig.  11 , where the striations started from a point at the end of CP 5. This fact suggests the beginning of a crack in the central region of the left edge, due to discontinuity on the surface of the specimen, which may have been generated due to the manufacturing processes used to produce the specimens. In images 7 and 8 of Fig.  15 , it is possible to observe the transition from the brittle fracture region to the ductile fracture. By enlarging images 1, 5, and 6 in Fig.  15 , it is possible to perceive the irregularity of the ductile fracture surface. Fig. 15 Images of the fracture section of SP6 obtained through SEM

The differences in the fatigue response can be associated with defects on the same specimen but also due to depositing the material with different conditions. Kanishka and Acherjee (Ref  52 ) evaluated the influence of torch oscillation in GMAW-WAAM-fabricated low-carbon steel using a voltage-controlled pulsed arc process (Iset = 218 A, Vset = 26.8 V, wire feed rate = 8 m/min, and 80%Ar-20%CO 2  shielding gas), and noted that the microstructure consisted of fine-grained ferritic phases, including acicular ferrite, polygonal/quasi-polygonal ferrite, lamellar pearlite, and bainite, due to the rapid cooling inherent to pulsed arc deposition and the additional grain refinement promoted by torch oscillation (2.5 mm amplitude and 4 Hz frequency), which enhances nucleation through dendrite fragmentation and melt pool convection, resulting in a more uniform grain distribution across the deposited layers; this refined and homogeneous microstructure added to it. Kanishka and Acherjee (Ref  52 ) reported improved mechanical performance associated with a refined and homogeneous microstructure (UTS increasing from 509.33 to 516.23 MPa and total elongation from 53.07 to 54.23% with torch oscillation). The present study exhibited an endurance limit of 302.04 MPa (≈ 52.5% Su), which is consistent with the expected fatigue strength being approximately half of the tensile strength.  Their study indicates that grain refinement and reduced porosity contribute to improved mechanical behavior and potentially enhanced fatigue resistance. Furthermore, the coarser microstructure observed in this work, dominated by polygonal ferrite and pearlite, contrasts with their fine-grained structure and may explain the greater sensitivity to defect-driven fatigue failure despite achieving a fatigue limit within the typical range.

The profile of the rupture region of SP6 is shown in Fig.  16 . It highlights the marks left by the sanding of the region from which the specimen was extracted, the same region where the specimen exhibited brittle fracture, with surface markings directly associated with crack propagation during the fatigue process, Fig.  15 . Fig. 16 Images of the rupture profile of SP6 obtained through SEM

In Region 1 (Fig.  17 ), the brittle fracture region is evident with parallel-oriented striations indicating crack growth perpendicular to this direction, pointing toward the end of the piece. Region 2, Fig.  17 (b), presents the transition region between the fracture mechanisms, delimited by the blue dashed line. In this figure, a structure similar to an inclusion (marked in red) is also observed in the dimple region, which may have originated in the deposition process. To confirm that such a location presents an inclusion, an analysis of the chemical composition of this structure would be necessary, as was carried out by Ayan and Kahraman (Ref  48 ), who identified MnO inclusions (via energy-dispersive x-ray spectroscopy analysis) in ER70S-6 specimens subjected to bending fatigue. Fig. 17 Details of SP6 (a) Region 1 and (b) Region 2

Rooprai et al. (Ref  53 ) studied the development of SS316-based claddings reinforced with 5% vanadium carbide (VC) deposited via WAAM-CMT on EN8 substrates and noted a significant improvement in microhardness (from 225 to 403 HV) and corrosion resistance, attributed to the uniform dispersion of VC particles acting as barriers to localized degradation and surface damage. The authors also observed that the presence of such reinforcing phases reduced the severity of surface defects, such as pitting, by limiting localized damage accumulation. This can be related to the present work, in which fatigue failure was consistently associated with crack initiation at defects such as pores, inclusions, and geometric discontinuities. Although no reinforcement was employed in the current study, the results similarly indicate that local microstructural features and defect distribution play a dominant role in controlling material performance, particularly under cyclic loading. Therefore, both studies highlight that improving microstructural homogeneity and minimizing defect severity are critical factors for enhancing the structural reliability of WAAM-CMT components.

Unlike the other specimens, SP1 did not exhibit a clear distinction between the striation (brittle) and dimple (ductile) regions. However, Fig.  18  shows a higher concentration of dimples in the upper region (image 7). This behavior is likely associated with the higher applied stress level, which was the highest among the tests (0.67 Su). Fig. 18 Images of the fracture section of SP1 obtained through SEM

The fracture profile of SP1, shown in Fig.  19 , also showed a different pattern: while in the other CPs elevation changes occurred laterally, elevation changes in SP1 were primarily between the upper and lower regions. Fig. 19 Images of the rupture profile of SP1 obtained through SEM

In Fig.  20 , a region consistent with brittle fracture mechanisms is observed, as well as striations oriented perpendicularly to the end of the piece, indicating that a crack may have started in this region. In Fig.  20 (b), a separation can be noted between the dimple region and the region in which there are signs of brittle fracture (delimited by the red dashed line), but without striations oriented in a parallel manner. As in Fig.  20 (a) and Fig.  20 (c) (Region 4), there are parallel striations, also indicating the beginning of a crack at this end of the piece. Fig. 20 Details of the fragile characteristics of SP1 (a) Region 1, (b) Region 2, and (c) Region 4

In Region 3, shown in Fig.  21 (a), a transition between brittle and ductile fracture regions can be identified, with striations still evident within areas where dimples are present. The striations propagate in multiple directions, indicating the presence of more than one crack in the specimen. Dimpled morphology is observed throughout the specimen, particularly in the upper portion, as shown in Fig.  21 (b), where the occurrence of this phenomenon is evident. In Fig.  21 (b), possible milling marks are also observed on the side of the piece (in red). Fig. 21 Details of SP1, (a) Region 3 and (b) Region 5

Overall, the SEM fractographic analysis revealed fatigue failure mechanisms consistent with those typically reported for high-strength low-alloy steels produced by wire-based additive manufacturing processes. Most specimens exhibited a well-defined sequence of crack initiation, stable propagation characterized by striations, and final rupture dominated by ductile fracture with dimple morphology. The clear separation between brittle and ductile regions observed in SP3, SP5, and SP6 indicates stable crack growth prior to final failure, with initiation frequently associated with surface or internal discontinuities, such as geometric stress concentrators, inclusions, or porosity from the deposition process. In contrast, specimen SP1, tested at the highest stress level, showed less distinct fracture region delimitation and a predominance of ductile features, indicating accelerated crack propagation and a reduced stable growth regime. These results confirm the strong influence of stress level and local defects on fatigue damage evolution in WAAM materials, highlighting the need for deposition control and post-processing strategies to limit defect formation and improve fatigue performance.

With a similar approach, Panchagade et al. (Ref  54 ) evaluated SS304L produced by CMT under monotonic Mode I fracture conditions using CT specimens and reported a fracture toughness of 61.41 MPa, approximately 17% higher than the conventional material (52.73 MPa), with fracture surfaces dominated by ductile features such as dimples. Besides the material differences, the behavior was similar. The present work observed that the final stage of fatigue failure in specimens SP3, SP5, and SP6 was also governed by ductile fracture, characterized by dimpled morphology following crack propagation marked by striations. This correspondence indicates that the underlying fracture mechanism remains ductile in both cases, with the difference being the presence of a stable crack growth stage under cyclic loading. The authors (Ref  54 ) also identified the presence of porosity in CMT specimens but reported no significant reduction in fracture toughness under monotonic loading. Differently, this work observed that pores, inclusions, and geometric discontinuities acted as preferential crack initiation sites, particularly in specimens tested at 316.8 MPa (SP3 and SP5) and 350 MPa (SP6), where striation regions originated from these defects. They attributed these differences to the higher sensitivity of fatigue behavior to local stress concentrations, where even small defects can control crack initiation and early propagation, unlike in monotonic fracture where global plasticity dominates.

Within the limitations of the work is the fact that the evaluation did not consider the different parts of the wall as a variable. Novelino et al. (Ref  55 ) evaluated the fatigue life of ER70S-6 steel produced by CMT-WAAM using a defect-based approach, combining defect mapping with Murakami’s √area method to analytically predict fatigue limits along the build height. The study reported a reduction in maximum defect size from 32.78 μm (lower region) to 19.09 μm (upper region), resulting in an increase in predicted fatigue limit from 208 to 228 MPa (≈ 9% variation). The results showed a clear correlation between thermal stabilization during deposition, reduced defect population, and improved fatigue resistance, highlighting the strong influence of defect size and distribution on fatigue behavior.

However, deposited parts with different distances from the substrate are being used, thus it is relevant to make this a complete wall evaluation. In this sense, the present work observed that the behavior of fatigue performance was similar to what Novelino et al. (Ref  55 ) observed; it is strongly governed by defects, with pores, inclusions, and geometric discontinuities acting as preferential crack initiation sites. In specimens tested at 316.8 MPa (SP3 and SP5) and 350 MPa (SP6), crack initiation was consistently associated with localized defects, followed by propagation characterized by striations and final ductile rupture. This agreement indicates that both the predicted fatigue limits in (Ref  55 ) and the experimentally observed failure mechanisms in this work are controlled by defect-driven crack initiation. This could be due to the intrinsic sensitivity of WAAM materials to process-induced discontinuities, which dominate fatigue behavior regardless of the specific evaluation method (analytical or experimental).

Another limitation resides in the fact that the fatigue results are based on a limited number of tests (six valid data points), which restricts the statistical robustness of the S-N curve. Although a consistent trendline was obtained ( R 2  = 0.91) with relatively low scatter (± 40%), the dataset is insufficient to define a reliable S-N curve or to accurately determine the fatigue limit. The absence of repeated tests at identical stress levels further limits the evaluation of variability and confidence intervals. Additionally, one specimen was reused (SP2), and its subsequent result was excluded due to prior fatigue damage, reducing the effective dataset. The adopted runout criterion of 10 6  cycles may also influence the estimation of the endurance limit, as higher cycle thresholds could lead to different interpretations. Finally, comparisons with literature are limited to qualitative analysis due to differences in deposition parameters and testing conditions. Therefore, the reported fatigue behavior and estimated fatigue limit should be interpreted as indicative rather than definitive.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: Based on the experimental investigation of fatigue behavior and fracture mechanisms of ER70S-6 steel deposited by WAAM using the CMT process, the following conclusions can be drawn: The fatigue response of the material exhibited a clear transition between finite and infinite life in the stress range between 316.8 MPa (0.55 Su) and 283.2 MPa (0.49 Su). Runout (10 6  cycles) was achieved at 283.2 and 302.04 MPa, indicating an endurance limit of approximately 302 MPa, corresponding to ≈ 52.5% of the ultimate tensile strength (Su). This value is consistent with classical fatigue estimations for low-alloy steels. The S-N curve presented a coherent trend ( R 2  = 0.91) with relatively low scatter (± 40%) despite the limited number of specimens, suggesting reasonable repeatability of the fatigue response under the investigated conditions. However, the dataset remains insufficient for robust statistical generalization. Fatigue performance was predominantly governed by defect-driven mechanisms, with crack initiation consistently associated with surface irregularities, geometric discontinuities, inclusions, and possible porosity. These features acted as local stress concentrators, significantly reducing fatigue life, indicating that fatigue resistance is primarily controlled by the defect population rather than intrinsic microstructural strength. Fractographic analysis revealed a typical fatigue failure sequence in most specimens (SP3, SP5, SP6), consisting of crack initiation at localized defects, stable crack propagation characterized by well-defined striations, and final fracture dominated by ductile dimple morphology. This confirms that the material exhibits classical fatigue behavior, with failure progression strongly influenced by process-induced discontinuities. The specimen tested at the highest stress level (384 MPa, 0.67 Su) exhibited a reduced distinction between crack propagation and final fracture regions, with a higher prevalence of ductile features. This indicates that increasing stress amplitude accelerates crack propagation and reduces the extent of stable fatigue crack growth. The measured microhardness (140.55 ± 36.36 HV) was lower than values reported in the literature (~200 HV for similar materials), which is attributed to the coarse ferrite–pearlite microstructure formed under reduced thermal gradients in the 100-layer wall. Despite this, fatigue performance remained within expected limits, reinforcing that the defect population has a more dominant effect than hardness in fatigue behavior. The results presented correspond exclusively to horizontally extracted specimens, representing in-layer properties. Therefore, the influence of build-direction anisotropy and interlayer boundaries was not assessed, limiting the generalization of the findings to components subjected to multi-directional loading.
